GelÅ«nas / BNS Under a new proposal from Lithuania's presidential palace, migrant workers who have lived and worked in the country for two years would be legally required to leave for six months â a rule that not only risks forcing them away but could also block them from family reunification and from ever gaining permanent residency. The following is an opinion piece by Dr. Skirmantas Bikelis, Senior research fellow at Law Institute of Lithuanian Centre for Social Sciences. Skirmantas Bikelis | V. Raupelio / LRT nuotr. How well people of different backgrounds live together is a complicated question â as complicated as society itself. Trying to sum up migrant integration and social wellbeing with a single number or percentage is not just imprecise, it can be actively misleading. Yet that is exactly what is happening in Lithuania's current immigration debate, and foreigners living here should understand what is being proposed and why. Earlier this spring, Vilnius mayor Valdas Benkunskas made himself something of a laughing stock among experts by announcing a supposedly scientifically-proven figure. According to him, once migrants reach 10% of a city's population, this marks a "tipping point" leading to the formation of migrant ghettos â and he used this claim to argue for stricter, migrant-unfriendly measures in the capital of Lithuania, where migrants already make up that proportion of the population. Sociologist Karolis Å½ibas, founder of the NGO Diversity Development Group, dismissed this, saying that Benkunskas' "10% tipping point" argument was plucked out of thin air, with no research to back it up. In reality, according to Å½ibas, ghettos or segregated neighbourhoods form because of factors like lack of affordable housing, housing discrimination, income inequality, or gaps in education, not because of any specific percentage of foreigners. Still, these are problems worth fixing regardless of how many migrants live in a country. A new figure, this time from the presidential palace Now a new, even smaller number has emerged â this time from the office of President Gitanas NausÄda â being used to justify tightening immigration rules further. Foreigners currently make up 7.5% of Lithuania's population, and the president's chief adviser, Vaidas AugustinaviÄius, argues this figure already needs to be "managed" and "restricted." At the president's initiative, the National Security Group within the presidential palace has drafted amendments to the Law on the Legal Status of Aliens. If passed, these changes could make it significantly harder for many labour migrants to build a stable life in Lithuania â and could even push existing migrant workers to leave, with little incentive to come back. Vaidas AugustinaviÄius | J. StaceviÄiaus / LRT nuotr. What's being proposed? First, the president is proposing to change how labour migrant quotas are calculated so that they include not only newly arriving migrants but also those continuing to work in Lithuania. This would sharply reduce â essentially by half â the quota available for new arrivals, unless the overall quota were doubled. It is not clear if that's happening any time soon. Secondly, perhaps the single most consequential change in the package: labour migrants would be required to leave Lithuania for at least six months after every two years of work. A presidential adviser, Evelina GudzinskaitÄ, has defended this by suggesting it simply gives workers a natural chance to visit family back home, in line with how their work cycles operate anyway. But this framing misses the real impact. Migrant workers can already visit their families whenever they choose - they don't need a forced six-month 'deportation' to do so. Worse still, under current Lithuanian law, migrant workers only gain the right to bring their families to live with them after two continuous years of legal residence. So, a mandatory six-month departure every two years would permanently block that right, meaning workers could never reach the residency threshold needed to bring their spouses or children to Lithuania. It would also prevent them from ever qualifying for permanent residency, which requires five continuous years in the country, and eventually citizenship. Lithuanian passport | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT Why family reunification matters - and why blocking it backfires EU law on family reunification recognises that living together as a family supports social stability and helps migrants integrate into their host country, which in turn benefits the wider economy and society. When families live together, money spent on housing and living costs stays in Lithuania rather than being sent abroad. Research in criminology also suggests people with family responsibilities are generally more likely to follow the law (as per Robert J Sampson and John H Laub's theory of informal social control). Blocking migrants from settling permanently or reuniting with their families would strip away their motivation to learn Lithuanian, put down roots, or build a long-term future here. As Ivanas Trunovas, a migration researcher at Diversity Development Group, puts it: "There is a worrying trend in Lithuania â rules are being tightened for both those already living here and new arrivals. This reduces their motivation to integrate and build a long-term life in the country. If we don't see newly arrived people as part of our shared future, and don't guarantee them opportunities, protection and access to services, the result will be that Lithuanian residents of foreign origin become less willing to integrate." The justification The explanatory note behind the proposal argues Lithuania has reached its limit on accepting migrants, that the country has not invested enough in integration services, and that a more "flexible" labour market requires higher turnover of foreign workers. This reasoning does not hold up well. Once again, attempting to justify strict anti-immigration measures with a particular figure (7.5%) makes for a rather flimsy argument. After all, the principle of "no person, no problem" belongs to undemocratic regimes, not a welfare state. And if integration services are indeed lacking, the answer is to fund and build them â not to close the door on migrants Lithuania actually needs. Notably, these restrictions are aimed squarely at labour migrants who create very few problems: people invited by Lithuanian employers, who have income, housing, and background checks from the police and security services already in place. What they typically need isn't extensive economic support, but basic cultural integration help â such as accessible language courses. That should not be difficult to provide. Yet it is precisely these workers - the ones actively sought out and needed by Lithuanian businesses - who are being targeted. Lithuanian language (associative image) | J. StaceviÄiaus / LRT nuotr. Aurelija MaldutytÄ, president of the Lithuanian Confederation of Employers, has pointed out that Lithuania has faced a decade-long shortage of long-haul lorry drivers, welders and other specialists that local workers simply won't take on. Annual quotas for hiring foreign staff already run out before the year ends. Despite this, the presidential palace wants to make it harder to bring in exactly the labour migrants the country badly needs. What's really driving this? So, the presidential palace's proposal appears to be bad for Lithuania's economy, and works against the welfare of migrant families and their prospects for successful integration. What, then, is really driving such proposals? The need for labour market flexibility, cited by the presidential adviser, hardly sounds like a sufficiently weighty reason. A more revealing comment came from employers' representative MaldutytÄ in a radio discussion, when she said many Lithuanians feel uneasy about foreign workers - not because of anything they've done, but because of unfamiliar language, culture, or religion. That discomfort appears to be borne out in survey data: research from the Lithuanian Centre for Social Sciences and Diversity Development Group found that only around half of Lithuanians would support the country accepting labour migrants from outside the EU, and a similar share said they would not want Muslims living in their neighbourhood. Yet there is no evidence that migrant workers or Muslims living in Lithuania are causing any significant problems. The unease seems rooted less in facts than in unfamiliarity and fears stoked by some commentators and politicians - including false claims that migration is "out of control" or drives up crime. If policy continues to be shaped by these sentiments rather than actual scientific evidence, the risk is a set of rules that damage both Lithuania's economy and the wellbeing of the society it is meant to protect â including the migrant families already contributing to it. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/19/un-c.text: More than 1,000 cases of sexual violence recorded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 involve victims as young as 4 and as old as 82 in a "shocking pattern of torture, intimidation and coercion," according to the report published on Friday by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights."I am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine," said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk.Both crimes were committed by Russian troops, who account for 89% of perpetrators in the 1,004 cases included in the report.While the majority of documented victims are men, particularly those held in places of detention, women and children have been most severely affected in occupied Ukrainian territory.Crimes against Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained medical workers include gang rape, genital mutilation and other acts of sexual humiliation.The most common single method recorded was the use of a Soviet-era military field telephone known as a "tapik" to administer electric shocks to the genitals: 155 cases, or 27% of the total, involved this form of abuse at least once, the report says.Individual survivor testimonies documented in the report include Ukrainian prisoners of war sexually assaulted with objects such as batons, cell door keys or shovel handles.A woman in Zaporizhzhia was raped several times a week for a month by a Russian soldier who promised better treatment for her detained husband. A woman in Kherson was assaulted nightly and repeatedly threatened with gang rape.In the Kyiv region, two Russian soldiers broke into a family home in 2022, shot and killed a woman's husband, then gang-raped her, threatening to shoot her in front of her four-year-old son if she resisted."Sexual violence is a grave feature of the full-scale armed attack against Ukraine. It must stop immediately, irrespective of the perpetrators," Türk said."Given the high prevalence of cases attributed to its forces, however, the Russian Federation in particular must take concrete and discernible steps to protect civilians and prisoners of war from all forms of torture, including sexual violence."The 20-page report covers the period from 24 February 2022 to the end of July 2026 and draws on confidential interviews with hundreds of victims, along with court documents and official records.Of the 11% of cases attributed to Ukrainian forces, nearly half involved threats of sexual violence against Russian prisoners of war and prisoners of war from third countries. The remainder included forced nudity, electric shocks and beatings to the genitals, sexually degrading treatment and two cases each of sexual assault and attempted rape.Conventions disregarded, withdrawn fromRussia was added to the UN Secretary-General's list of parties credibly suspected of committing sexual violence in conflict in May of this year — a list that includes Sudan, Somalia and Haiti as repeat offenders. The Kremlin rejected the findings as politically motivated.The UN Human Rights Council's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has separately documented widespread use of torture by Russian authorities against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war in occupied territory and inside Russia.Russia formally withdrew from the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture in September 2025 following its expulsion from the Council of Europe, ending visits by European monitors to Russian detention facilities.Russia remains a formal party to the UN Convention Against Torture and prohibits torture under its constitution and criminal code.The Ukrainian foreign ministry welcomed the report, saying it had "once again demonstrated the scale of systematic human rights violations committed by the Russian Federation."Rape and sexual violence were codified as war crimes and crimes against humanity under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, which entered into force in 2002.The use of systematic rape as a weapon of war was first formally prosecuted as a crime against humanity and an act of genocide by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s.

Kennedy, Jr. Sunetra Gupta Tony Robbins Victor Davis Hanson Space Vaccines Africa Africa Archives South Africa Libya Egypt Kenya Sudan Niger AFRICOM South America South America Archives Brazil Venezuela Argentina Columbia Bolivia Chile Nord Stream Trials: Problems Appear in Germany’s Andromeda Story Freddie Ponton 21st Century Wire The Nord Stream sabotage has produced years of claims, leaks and competing theories, but only recently have two formal legal records begun to show what can be tested in court. In Germany, federal prosecutors have charged Ukrainian national Serhii Kuznietsov over the pipeline explosions. Meanwhile, in London, Nord Stream AG sued Lloyd’s Insurance Company S.A. and Arch Insurance (EU) DAC after insurers refused to pay for the damage; the Commercial Court’s judgment examined the attack in technical detail without deciding who carried it out. The London proceedings were not intended to identify the perpetrators. Their purpose was to determine whether the insurers’ war exclusion applied. The court heard extensive forensic and operational evidence, yet many of the questions raised by Nord Stream AG’s experts receded once the judge concluded that the exclusion applied under any plausible account of the attack. The judgment settled the insurance claim without identifying the perpetrators or settling what happened at the Nord Stream blast sites on the Baltic seabed in September 2022. The German proceedings claim to go further by identifying an alleged participant. Yet the publicly disclosed case has not established that the Andromeda was present above every blast site, matched evidence recovered from the yacht to material from the seabed, or explained how the operation was carried out. The London court found that it did not need to identify the perpetrators, while German prosecutors have yet to prove their case against Ukrainian national Serhii Kuznietsov, whom they accuse of participating in the sabotage. More importantly, the evidence heard in London exposed why Germany’s yacht story is taking on water. Prosecutors have a boat, a crew and a theory, but no publicly demonstrated forensic bridge to the Baltic seabed. IMAGE: Gas breaks the surface above the Nord Stream 2 leak south of Dueodde, Bornholm, on 27 September 2022. Danish Defence aircraft documented the disturbance as authorities established exclusion zones around the pipeline leaks (Source: Danish Defence/ Forsvaret ) Almost four years after a series of underwater explosions tore through the Nord Stream pipelines near the Danish island of Bornholm, the German prosecution and the London insurance trial have presented two very different versions of the event before the public. Germany claims that a covert Ukrainian military team sailed into the Baltic Sea aboard a 50-foot charter sailing yacht, dove down to four pipelines and planted charges, under orders from Ukrainian state agencies. Conversely in London, after six weeks of deliberation—including evidence on explosives, subsea operations and the damage itself, the court ruled without deciding who carried out the attack. However, the insurance trial has introduced some compelling evidence which could potentially refine the facts of this story. Two competing narratives Germany’s Federal Prosecutor indicted Ukrainian national Serhii Kuznietsov in Hamburg on 30 June 2026, accusing him of coordinating the team aboard Andromeda . On 6 July, the Commercial Court in London rejected Nord Stream AG’s insurance claim after finding that the sabotage fell within a war exclusion—a conclusion the judge could reach whether the attacker was assumed to be from Ukraine, Russia or the United States. More crucially, the London’s judgment leaves behind a highly credible and substantial technical record, one which presents serious difficulties for the German trial’s version of events. The forensic experts examined explosions at two groups of sites, separated by roughly six and a half kilometres, and over a time window of 17 hours, rupturing three pipeline strings, and damaging a fourth, although without opening it, and leaving another area of explosive damage known as “the Dent”. The German narrative attributes the explosion pattern to four devices weighing at least 14 kilograms each, carried aboard Andromeda and somehow placed by said divers at depths of approximately 70 to 80 metres, according to the Federal Prosecutor’s announcement . The London experts’ analysis is much more precise and backed up by forensic data, and points to a number of technical disagreements Germany, namely about about the number of explosive charges, the nature of “the Dent”, and the mechanics of the damage, which are recorded in the materials and explosives joint memorandum . MAP: Nord Stream Explosion Sites and the NS1 Line 2 Dent – four primary Nord Stream explosion sites near Bornholm Island, with the separate NS1 Line 2 “Dent” shown approximately 90 meters from the adjacent NS1 Line 1 rupture; pipeline spacing is schematic (Source: 21WIRE) Much of the evidence needed to test that account remains spread across separate investigations and private surveys. Swedish and Danish authorities maintained controlled over those blast areas before Nord Stream AG was allowed to inspect them, while German material entered the London proceedings under sealed confidentiality. Securing the crime scene became even more complicated due to the fact that a Norwegian offshore vessel known as the Normand Frontier , later spent days working across the pipeline sites for a client whose identity has not been publicly disclosed, according to the London judgment . Later in this report, we will present our own commercial reconstruction of this vessel’s movements based on the actual AIS vessel data, and a possible motive for deploying this mystery vessel. The story of yacht Andromeda brings together a number of disparate pieces of evidence and storylines; a secret Baltic voyage, false identities, diving equipment, and trace residues of RDX and HMX explosives, according to Germany’s Federal Court decision . Still, the public case stops short of showing how those findings correspond to the devices and the actual damage recovered from the Baltic seabed. That missing connection means that the Hamburg proceedings falls wide of the mark—because the evidence revealed in London went much further in terms of closing the gap between the technical demands of the attack and the actual post-blast site forensics. It also showed how much of the original crime scene record remained beyond the reach of the experts who testified, and how many unanswered questions still surround the authorities and vessels that reached that seabed long before the evidence was assembled for these two legal proceedings. DOCUMENT: Nord Stream’s Unresolved Evidence: Court Records, Vessel Data and Unanswered Questions After the London Judgment and Germany’s First Indictment (Source; Author) Nord-Streams-Unresolved-Evidence- Two explosions, four lines Nord Stream consisted of four large underwater pipeline strings running from Russia, through the Baltic Sea, to Germany. Nord Stream 1 had two operational strings, while the two Nord Stream 2 lines had been completed without entering into full commercial service, and the London claim concerned Nord Stream 1, even though damage to both systems formed part of the evidence. The first seismic event was registered at 2.03am local time on 26 September 2022, and corresponded to damage south-east of Bornholm in the Denmark’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). Nord Stream 2 Line A ruptured, while Line B suffered external damage without leaking. Seventeen hours later, at 7.03pm, a second event struck north-east of Bornholm, rupturing both Nord Stream 1 pipeline strings at locations in the both the Swedish and Danish EEZ areas, as detailed in the London judgment . The experts in London agreed that directional or shaped charges had been used to focus explosive force against the pipes, and that the explosive was RDX-based. Their reconstruction began with an initial penetration of the pipe’s steel wall, followed by violent movement and decompression as the gas escaped, further enlarging the breaches and contributing to the extensive destruction visible during later surveys, according to the London record . The results were not uniform. Three strings ruptured, but Nord Stream 2 Line B remained sealed despite external damage, and a later survey found another area of deformation on Nord Stream 1 Line 2, referred to in court as “the Dent”. Nord Stream AG suggested that an anchor might have caused it, although the absence of a corresponding drag scar led the judge to find, on the evidence and following cross-examination, that it was more likely that this resulted from an explosion as part of the same attack, according to the London judgment . This was a judicial finding on ‘anchor-versus-explosive’ causation, not an expert consensus on the precise explosive mechanism, which remains disputed between testimonies of Rigby and Pettitt/Lumley. The materials experts’ points of agreement and disagreement are set out in the materials and explosives joint memorandum , with further analysis contained in Rigby’s supplemental report and Pettitt’s supplemental report . However, one important point was agreed on by the experts: they concluded that directional, or shaped charges were used, and that the devices were housed in pre-made sealed containers specifically designed for underwater use at depth, and that the explosives were RDX-based. They disagreed over the precise configuration. Professor Rigby considered a linear shaped charge most likely, while Dr Pettitt and Hefin Jones favoured a three-dimensional shaped charge. At another Nord Stream 1 location, the operator described one end of the ruptured pipe as mangled and heavily deformed while the other appeared comparatively smooth. The London judgment recorded the difference without deciding what caused it, leaving an open question as to whether or not the contrast arose from the number and position of the placed charges, the direction of force, movement of the pipe, or subsequent interaction with the seabed. Contrast this level of detail in the London case with Germany’s basic public account that makes a general reference to four charges placed on three pipeline strings, according to the Federal Prosecutor’s announcement . The London evidence describes explosive damage across four strings and includes “the Dent”—which does not fit neatly into the published German sequence. A reconstruction presented in Hamburg will therefore have to place each alleged device at a particular location and show how four placements produced the separate damage patterns recorded across two separate pipeline systems. What London decided The London proceeding arose from Nord Stream AG’s claim for approximately €580 million under policies covering damage to its two pipeline strings. The insurers relied on exclusions for losses connected with “war” and “acts of government”, which allowed the court to decide the case by examining whether the sabotage had the required relationship to the war between Russia and Ukraine, according to the London judgment . IMAGE: The London Commercial Court, housed in The Rolls Building, where Nord Stream AG’s €580 million insurance claim was decided (Image Source: Wikimedia ) The court heard competing assessments of possible Ukraine, Russia and United States involvement, whose possible motives changed according to when planning was assumed to have begun. The experts disagreed about relative likelihood, and one who placed Ukraine ahead of the other candidates still could not say that Ukrainian responsibility was more likely than not, as the London court recorded. The judge did not need to resolve those disagreements because the “war exclusion” applied under each of the principal scenarios. References to the Andromeda sailboat and the German investigation appeared as background to the insurance arguments rather than any definitive finding that a Ukrainian crew aboard the yacht had carried out the sabotage, according to the London judgment . Some German investigative documents were disclosed to the parties under court-ordered confidentiality and remained outside the public court filings. At the same time, the London experts never received the complete findings from the early Swedish and Danish crime scene inspections, which meant that an unusually detailed examination of the attack still proceeded from only part of the evidence held by the various authorities, according to the court record . The voyage of Andromeda German prosecutors said that an intermediary actor obtained the Andromeda yacht by using false identity documents and specifically requested a yacht without an Automatic Identification System (AIS). Moreover, a vessel of its size had no legal obligation to transmit AIS data , and the request by the intermediary actor would have ensured that its route did not appear continuously on public vessel-tracking services. IMAGE: The sailing yacht Andromeda in the Baltic Sea photographed during a later reconstruction voyage by German media outlets DER SPIEGEL and ZDF (Source: Der Spiegel ) Kuznietsov allegedly travelled from Ukraine through Poland and entered Germany on 4 September 2022 using a forged Ukrainian passport carrying his photograph. By 8 September, according to Germany’s Federal Court , he had joined six other people in the harbour of Wiek on Rügen, where the alleged team of seven persons consisted of a skipper, an explosives specialist, four divers and Kuznietsov as coordinator. The German Federal Prosecutor’s announcement says they sailed towards Bornholm with diving equipment and military explosives, then placed four timed charges on three pipeline strings in both the Danish and Swedish exclusive economic zones. Each device is said to have weighed at least 14 kilograms and contained RDX and HMX. The crew allegedly returned to Rügen, where Kuznietsov left the yacht on 23 September before travelling through Poland to Ukraine, three days before the explosions. Using a combination of data points, investigators are said to have reconstructed the voyage without a logbook, or continuous AIS track, by using harbour records, witness accounts, coastal surveillance and navigation data, according to the Federal Court decision .
